e.t: Abana, also called Avana, is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a particular named place or feature rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The word appears once in the LXX, in 2 Kings 5:12. Its exact significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the lexical sense itself is simply the name Abana or Avana.

This adjective describes someone or something that is without harm—safe, harmless, or not causing injury. It expresses the absence of damaging effects rather than naming a particular action or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in the book of Wisdom. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains freedom from harm or injury.

Slumberlessness means a state of having no sleep or being unable to sleep. It is a noun describing sleeplessness as a condition, rather than an action or a person. In the Greek LXX corpus, this word occurs nine times, all in the deuterocanonical writings, with eight occurrences in Sirach and one in 2 Maccabees. Its precise significance in any individual passage depends on the surrounding context.

Adia is a proper name, also rendered Athia. It identifies a person rather than expressing a general action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears twice, both times in genealogical material in 1 Chronicles. The available wording does not provide a separate descriptive meaning for the name, so it is best understood simply as the personal name Adia or Athia. Its precise reference is determined by the genealogy in each passage.

This proper noun means “Aithiops” or “Ethiops,” serving as a name or designation rather than a general action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 28 times across 26 verses, so it is a recurring identifying term within that corpus. Its precise reference in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself remains a proper name or designation. It occurs from Numbers through Zephaniah, including passages in Chronicles, Psalms, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel.

This word is a proper name, referring to someone called “Amouēl” or “Amoil.” It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 4:26. Because the available wording does not include the verse text or surrounding passage, the name itself does not provide further information about the person’s identity, role, or significance. Its basic function is simply to identify an individual by name in that genealogical passage.

This verb means to announce—to make information known or report something to others. It describes the act of communicating a message, news, or fact rather than keeping it private. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 214 times, showing that announcing is a recurring action in many kinds of passages. The precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being communicated and to whom.

Anathōthi, also rendered Anathothi, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It appears twice in the LXX corpus, both times in 1 Chronicles. The available information identifies the name but does not establish whether it refers to a person, place, or another named entity. Its precise reference therefore depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The name occurs in 1 Chronicles 11:28 and 1 Chronicles 12:3.

This word means “rejection” or “refusal.” As a noun, it describes the act of turning something down or declining to accept it. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalm 72:4. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central idea remains a deliberate refusal or rejection rather than simple absence or inability. The word therefore points to an expressed act of declining, opposing, or withholding acceptance.

This word means an “offering”: something presented or given to God. It is a noun that names the gift or presentation itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Numbers 4:19 and Psalms 50:21, showing the same central meaning in both passages. The surrounding verse determines what is offered and why, but the word itself points to the offering being presented.

This adjective describes something that cannot be cured or healed—“incurable.” It can describe a condition, wound, or destructive situation whose damage is not naturally remedied. The word occurs nine times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Scripture corpus, including passages from Deuteronomy, Job, Proverbs, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what the surrounding passage identifies as incurable.

This Greek LXX verb means “measure against.” It describes assessing one thing by setting it against another measure, standard, or point of comparison. The word functions as an action, focusing on the act of weighing or comparing rather than on the object being measured. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 7:6. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This adjective describes someone as “undisciplined.” It points to a person who lacks the ordered, teachable character associated with discipline. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, it occurs 17 times, appearing especially in Proverbs and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains a description of someone not governed by discipline or instruction.

This Greek LXX verb means “block up” or “stop up”—to close something so that movement or passage is prevented. It describes an action rather than a person or object. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, once in Lamentations and once in 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and what is being closed, but its central idea remains shutting off or obstructing passage.

This noun refers to a “chief cup-bearing” official—a person identified by responsibility for serving or bearing the cup. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at Genesis 40:13, so its use is rare in this corpus. The word names an office or role rather than an action, quality, or general object. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the way the role functions there.

Asith is a proper name, preserved as “Asith” rather than translated into a descriptive word. In the Greek Septuagint (LXX), it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 7:33. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not provided here, the name’s particular role in that verse cannot be explained further from this word entry alone. Its ordinary lexical meaning is therefore the name “Asith.”

This word means “childlessness”: the condition of having no children. As a noun, it names that state rather than describing an action. It points to a condition, not to a person, place, object, or event. In this LXX corpus, it occurs four times across both Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings. Its central idea remains the absence of children, while its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

This word means “spindle,” a tool used in spinning thread or yarn. It is a noun naming a physical implement rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 31:19. The word’s basic meaning is therefore concrete and specific: it identifies the slender tool associated with turning fibers into thread. Its exact significance in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage, but the word itself refers to the spindle as an object.

This adverb means acting “unsparingly; without mercy.” It describes an action carried out freely and without holding back, especially when kindness, pity, or restraint might otherwise limit what is done. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, it occurs three times: once in Proverbs and twice in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any individual sentence depends on the action it modifies, but its central idea remains clear: something is done without sparing or showing mercy.

Achsan, also rendered Akhsan, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, in Joshua 15:16 and Joshua 15:17. Because it is a proper name, its basic meaning is the person’s designation; the surrounding verse supplies any further information about that person or the event. It should therefore be understood as a name preserved in the biblical account, not expanded into an additional concept or definition.

Baldad is a proper name, also rendered Valthath. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies one of the named people associated with the book of Job. The name occurs six times, all within Job, from Job 2:11 through Job 42:17. Because it is a personal name rather than a descriptive word, its meaning is primarily identification: it points to Baldad himself rather than expressing an action, quality, or idea.

This is a proper name, given as “Bēbi; Vivi.” It identifies a named person rather than describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 7:16. Because it is a personal name, its ordinary meaning is chiefly its identifying function; the available lexical information does not provide an additional descriptive sense or explanation of the name’s origin.

“Grind” means to crush or break something by rubbing or pressing it repeatedly, and this word functions as a verb describing that action. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs five times, each in a different verse. Its basic sense is physical and active rather than a name or description of an object. The surrounding verse determines what is being ground and how the action contributes to the sentence.

This adjective describes someone as gluttonous—marked by excessive or uncontrolled appetite for food. It functions as a description rather than naming an action or object, so it characterizes a person or their conduct in terms of eating. In the Greek LXX material represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 2:7. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine precisely how the description functions there.

This adjective describes something as earth-like or earthy—belonging to, resembling, or arising from the earth. It presents an earthly quality rather than naming a person or action. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in the Wisdom literature. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning remains a description of earth-related character or substance.

This adjective describes something dark or gloomy. It refers to a lack of light or to an atmosphere marked by heaviness and obscurity, rather than expressing an action or a person’s name. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Exodus and Proverbs, so its basic sense is clear while its precise force depends on the surrounding sentence. The word is rendered “dark” in Exodus 19:16. [p03:word:lxx:L703133:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L703133:occurrences] [p01:word:lxx:L703133:reference:0]

This verb means “have full strength” or be “quite sufficient.” It describes having enough ability, strength, or resources to continue or meet a need. As a verb, it points to a condition of adequacy rather than merely possessing something. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 2:26; the surrounding verse is needed to determine how that basic idea applies there.

This word describes something interwoven with gold, emphasizing gold worked into or woven through it rather than merely placed beside it. It can function as a descriptive word for an object or material. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice: once in Psalms and once in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central meaning remains “interwoven with gold.”

This noun means “thirst,” the physical desire or need for water. In the Greek Old Testament, it names the condition of being thirsty rather than an action or a person. The word occurs 15 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented in this corpus, including passages from Deuteronomy, Psalms, Isaiah, and 4 Maccabees. Its repeated use across these writings shows a straightforward bodily meaning, while the surrounding verse determines how the condition fits the particular statement.

This noun refers to a person who receives bribes—someone who accepts gifts or payments in exchange for improper influence or favor. It describes the person by what he does, not merely someone who happens to possess money or receive an ordinary gift. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Proverbs 15:27. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding proverb, but its basic meaning clearly identifies corrupt receiving for personal gain.

This verb expresses being “involved in” something. It describes participation or engagement rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times: once in Proverbs and twice in Sirach. Because no verse text is provided, the surrounding passage is needed to determine what the word specifically involves in each occurrence. Its core meaning remains participation in something.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “lead in” or “bring in.” It describes moving a person, animal, or group into a place or situation, with the action focused on guiding or causing entry. As a verb, it expresses what someone does rather than naming a person or thing. It occurs 143 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical books represented here, so it is a regularly used action word rather than a rare expression. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being brought in and where.

This Greek LXX verb means “fall out” or “fall off.” It describes something moving out of its place, dropping away, or becoming detached. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming a person or thing. The word occurs 29 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, where its precise force depends on what is falling and the surrounding sentence. Its central idea remains departure from a position or attachment, whether by falling downward or coming away from something.

This Greek LXX noun means “outflow” or “pouring out.” It describes something being released from one place so that it flows or is poured outward. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish Scripture, appearing once each in Leviticus, 1 Kings, and Sirach. Its precise reference may involve different substances or situations, but its central idea remains movement outward through flowing or being poured out.

This verb means “make glorious”: to bring honor, splendor, or recognized greatness to someone or something. It describes an action that causes glory to be displayed or acknowledged, rather than merely possessing glory. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 11 times, chiefly in the Old Testament portion of the Greek Scriptures. Its use includes passages in Exodus, Ezekiel, and the Psalms, showing that the word can describe God’s acts or the honor given within human affairs.

This verb means “make,” describing the act of producing or carrying something out. It presents making as an action rather than as a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 14:40. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine exactly what is being made or done there, but the word itself centers on making or accomplishing something. Its single occurrence means the broader range of its use cannot be established from this corpus alone.

This noun means an embalmer, a person whose work is to prepare a dead body for burial by treating it so it can be preserved. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Genesis 50:2, in the account of preparing Jacob’s body. The word identifies the worker rather than the treatment itself. Its meaning is therefore a specific occupational title connected with caring for the dead after death and before burial.

This Greek word means “enumerate”: to count or list things one by one. As a verb, it describes the act of carefully reckoning a number or making a complete count rather than referring to things generally. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 20 times, including passages about counting descendants, people, or other measurable things. The precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being counted, but the central idea remains a deliberate, item-by-item reckoning.

This verb means “set at naught”: to treat someone or something as having no value, authority, or importance. It describes an act of disregarding, rejecting, or counting something as nothing. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used 48 times, so it can describe more than one kind of disregard while retaining this central idea. Its exact force in a particular passage depends on what person, authority, or thing is being treated as insignificant.

This Greek LXX verb means “rattle over.” It describes an action involving a rattling sound passing over or across something. The word appears five times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, with occurrences in Proverbs, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Amos, and Sirach. Because the actual verse wording and surrounding passages are not provided here, the precise object or situation affected by the rattling must be determined from each verse’s context. Its basic sense remains an active movement or sound expressed by the verb.

This Greek LXX verb means to come to the surface or float. It describes something moving upward until it appears on top of, or remains upon, water or another surrounding substance. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 2 Kings 6:6. Its basic sense is a physical movement from below to the surface, while the surrounding verse determines the precise force of the word in that passage.

This word means “say; speak,” referring to expressing words aloud or communicating something in speech. It is a verb, so it describes the act of speaking rather than a person, place, or thing. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs 378 times, showing that it is a common word for reported speech and spoken communication. Its precise force in any passage depends on what is being said and who is speaking, but its central sense remains the simple act of saying or speaking.

This Greek LXX verb means “stick fast” or “support.” It describes holding firmly, fastening something in place, or providing the support needed to remain secure. The word appears ten times in the Greek Old Testament, especially in Proverbs, where its sense concerns firm reliance and stability. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person or object. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on what is being held, attached, or supported in that passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “dress” or “attire,” referring to clothing worn by a person. It names outward garments rather than an action or personal quality. The word appears twice in the Greek LXX material represented here, both times in 2 Maccabees. Its precise significance in either occurrence depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense remains clothing or what someone wears.

This adjective means “beneficent”: actively doing good and bringing helpful results to others. It describes a person, quality, or action marked by generosity and practical kindness rather than mere good intentions. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Wisdom 7:23. Because the verse text is not provided, the word’s exact force in that sentence must be understood from its surrounding context, but its central sense remains someone or something that benefits others.

This adjective describes someone who can be appeased readily—that is, receptive to calming, reconciliation, or a request for peace. It presents the person as not stubbornly resistant when approached for settlement. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 5:13. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning is someone who is easily placated or willing to be reconciled.

This noun means “ready obedience”: a willing, prompt response to rightful instruction or authority. It describes more than outward compliance; it emphasizes a disposition prepared to obey. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times, all in 4 Maccabees. The exact force in any individual passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains obedience offered readily rather than reluctantly.

Zakanaim is a proper name, rendered also as “Zakanem.” It identifies a named location or designation in the Greek Old Testament, rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. The name occurs once, in Joshua 15:56, so its exact significance depends on the surrounding passage and the place or person being listed there. Its form functions as a name, not as a general word with a broader everyday meaning.

Thamnathasachara, also rendered Thamnathasakhara, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named person or place in the Greek Old Testament tradition, but the available lexical information does not specify which. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Joshua 24:31. Its precise referent must therefore be determined from the surrounding verse and passage, not from the name itself.

This word means “foundation”: the supporting base on which something is built or established. It functions as a noun when naming that foundation and can describe something connected with a foundation. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 41 times, showing regular use for structural foundations and other foundational settings. Its central idea remains the firm underlying support that gives a structure stability.

Ieddouran, also rendered Ieththuran, is a personal name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a particular individual rather than expressing a general idea, action, or quality. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at 2 Samuel 8:10. The available lexical information gives the name itself but does not provide an additional meaning or description of the person. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

This verb means “refresh”: to restore freshness, strength, or renewed vitality. In the Greek Old Testament, it describes an action done to something or someone, rather than a person or object itself. The word occurs twice in the Greek text of Sirach, appearing once in Sirach 35:8 and once in Sirach 43:22. Its basic meaning remains focused and consistent: bringing renewal or relief so that what has been affected becomes fresh again. The surrounding verse determines whether the refreshing concerns a person, condition, or created thing.

This adjective describes someone or something as “equal to the gods” or “godlike.” It expresses resemblance to divine beings or a status viewed as comparable to theirs, rather than naming a god itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 9:12. The surrounding verse is needed to determine precisely how the description functions there, but the word’s central sense is a comparison with the gods.

Iōyan; Iuan is a proper name used to identify an individual in the Greek Old Testament. Its meaning is therefore its name designation rather than a descriptive quality, action, or abstract idea. The name occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing in Genesis and 1 Chronicles. Because no verse text or wider context is provided here, the name’s specific genealogical or narrative role must be understood from the passage where it appears.

This Greek LXX verb means “fully arm,” describing the act of equipping someone completely for a task or conflict. It presents arming as an intentional action, not merely possessing weapons. The word occurs nine times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing once in Jeremiah and eight times in the Deuterocanonical books. Its central idea remains practical and direct: to provide the equipment needed for readiness or action. The surrounding passage determines whether the subject is arming another person, preparing people generally, or describing someone as equipped.

This verb means “cover”: to place something over another thing or cause it to be covered. It describes an action rather than an object, and its basic sense remains the same across the Greek Old Testament and related writings. The word occurs 81 times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing especially in Exodus, Psalms, Numbers, and Ezekiel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being covered and the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX verb means “eat up” or “devour.” It describes consuming something completely or thoroughly, whether the sentence presents the action plainly or uses it in a broader comparison. The word occurs six times in the LXX corpus, appearing in both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being consumed and the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX verb means “bend down” or “stoop.” It describes lowering oneself or moving downward rather than remaining upright. As a verb, it expresses an action, so its meaning centers on the movement of bending or stooping. It occurs once in the Greek LXX, at 2 Kings 9:32. The word names a physical action, not an object or person. The surrounding passage determines exactly who or what is bending in that occurrence.

This Greek LXX verb means “retain”: to keep something rather than let it go. It describes an action, showing what someone does with something that remains in their possession or under their care. In the LXX, it occurs three times, in Genesis 39:16, 2 Samuel 5:21, and 1 Kings 18:18. The surrounding wording determines what is being retained in each passage, but the central idea remains keeping or holding on to it.

This Greek verb means “plant”: to put a plant into the ground or establish it so that it can grow. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or place. The word appears 23 times in the LXX corpus, including passages from Exodus, Leviticus, Psalms, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Amos. Its basic meaning remains focused on planting, while the surrounding verse determines whether the action is literal or carries a broader image.

This noun refers to a teller of false tales—a person characterized by spreading stories that are untrue. It names the person who tells such tales rather than describing the tale itself. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs once, in Proverbs 33:22. Its basic sense is therefore focused and specific: a false-tale teller. The surrounding verse is needed to explain how this person functions in that particular passage.

The word is a proper name, rendered “Kephira” or “Kefira.” It functions as a name rather than a general descriptive term. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both in Joshua, at Joshua 9:17 and Joshua 18:24. Since the available lexical information gives the name but not the verse text or contextual details, its precise referent in each passage must be determined from the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “thread,” referring to a strand used as a tangible material. Its basic sense is simple and concrete rather than describing an action, quality, or person. It occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, once in Numbers 15:38 and once in Sirach 6:30. The word’s precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse text, but its ordinary lexical meaning remains thread.

This word means “basket,” referring to a container used for carrying or holding things. It is a noun with a straightforward physical meaning rather than an abstract quality or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Judges and once in Psalms, with the singular idea also appearing in a plural rendering. Its precise role in either verse depends on the surrounding context, but the word itself identifies a basket or similar carrying container.

The word means “circling; in a circle,” describing movement around something or a position surrounding it. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical books to express a circular arrangement or surrounding direction. It occurs 227 times in the LXX corpus, so readers may encounter it in varied settings, while its central idea remains circular movement or position.

This adjective describes something as functional or ministerial—connected with carrying out an assigned service or duty. It can characterize an object, role, or activity according to its practical use in serving a required purpose. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, especially in passages concerning the tabernacle, its furnishings, and the work associated with worship and service. Its precise application depends on the surrounding verse, but its central sense remains something arranged for service or functioning in a ministry.

This Greek LXX verb means “lengthen”: to make something longer or extend its reach or duration. As a verb, it describes an action or change rather than a person, object, or quality. The word appears 21 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, including Psalms, Ecclesiastes, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being lengthened and the surrounding sentence.

Masēa, also rendered Masia, is a personal name rather than a common word describing an object, action, or quality. As a proper noun in the Greek Old Testament, it identifies an individual by name. It occurs once in this corpus, in Ezra 10:30. The name itself does not provide a broader definition or spiritual concept; its precise significance depends on the person and surrounding passage in that reference.

Melchias is a personal name, preserved in English as “Melchias.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), this name occurs five times, appearing three times in Nehemiah and twice in Jeremiah. The name itself does not provide enough information to identify one single person across every occurrence; the surrounding passage determines whom it names.

This noun means “exchange” or “barter”—the giving of one thing in return for another. It names a transaction or trade rather than an action of speaking, feeling, or believing. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Sirach 37:11, so its ordinary lexical sense is clear even though the surrounding verse is not included here. The word points to reciprocal dealing in goods or value.

Miamin is a personal name. It identifies an individual in the Greek Old Testament tradition rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears twice in the LXX corpus, once in 1 Chronicles 24:9 and once in Nehemiah 10:8. Without the surrounding verse text, Scripture does not provide enough context here to explain more about the person bearing this name or the role connected with either occurrence.

This proper name refers to the Nabataioi, also rendered Navatei, a named people in the Greek Old Testament tradition. It functions as a people’s name rather than a description of an action, quality, or abstract idea. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 1 Maccabees 5:25. Without the verse text, its broader role in that sentence cannot be described more specifically, but its basic meaning is the name of this people.

Noa is a proper name, identifying the person called Noa. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears once, at 1 Chronicles 8:2. The name itself is not presented as a descriptive word for an action, quality, or object. It functions as a personal designation, and its precise significance in that single verse depends on the surrounding passage rather than on a broader repeated usage.

Oza is a proper name used to identify people in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a descriptive word with a broader lexical meaning; its ordinary function is simply to name a person. The name occurs 14 times in 12 verses in the LXX, including passages in Numbers, 2 Samuel, 2 Kings, and 1 Chronicles. The surrounding context determines which individual named Oza is meant in each passage.

This LXX word is a proper noun, meaning it functions as a personal or place name rather than as a general description. Its lexical meaning is given as “Onom.” It occurs twice in the Greek LXX, both times in Joshua 15:8. The available information identifies its naming function, but does not provide enough verse text to explain which person or place it names in that passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “haven,” referring to a sheltered place where a person or vessel can find protection or rest. It occurs twice in this corpus: once in Genesis and once in 4 Maccabees. Its basic sense remains that of a secure harbor or refuge, while the surrounding verse determines whether the word refers more directly to a physical place or uses that idea in a broader way.

This noun means a scar or mark—a visible sign left on the skin. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used for marks considered when examining skin conditions in Leviticus. Its basic sense is physical: a scar, blemish-like mark, or other visible change on the body. The word occurs seven times, all in Leviticus 13–14, so its recorded use is concentrated in instructions about recognizing and evaluating such marks.

This noun means “rear,” referring to the back part or position of something. It identifies what is behind rather than in front, helping describe location or arrangement. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Deuteronomy and once in Joshua. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its ordinary sense remains the rear or back area.

This adjective means “in all kinds of melodies,” describing something expressed or performed through varied musical tunes. It points to breadth within melody rather than to one particular song or musical style. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 7:16. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense concerns variety in melodies.

This verb means to incite: to stir someone or a group toward a particular action or response. It describes an active effort to move others, rather than merely doing something oneself. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical books represented here, it occurs eight times, beginning in Deuteronomy and continuing through Sirach. Its exact force in a verse depends on who is being moved and what response follows.

This Greek LXX verb means to carry someone or something along with another person, or to escort them. It describes accompanying or transporting someone rather than merely carrying an object independently. The word occurs seven times in the Greek text of 2 Maccabees, across six verses, so its basic sense is consistent but its precise role depends on the surrounding sentence. Its meaning remains centered on taking someone along, conveying them, or accompanying them from one place to another.

This noun means a provocation—something that stirs anger or gives someone cause for anger. It can describe an act or circumstance that incites resentment rather than anger itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in the books of 1 Kings and 2 Chronicles. Its central idea is an offense or deliberate cause that arouses anger. The surrounding passage determines what particular action or situation is being described in each occurrence.

“Fifth” means coming after the fourth in an ordered series. This adjective identifies a person, thing, time, or position as number five, helping readers recognize sequence or order. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 59 times, with the same basic numerical meaning throughout. It appears in passages ranging from Genesis and Leviticus to Kings, Chronicles, and later writings. Its precise reference—what is fifth—depends on the surrounding words in each sentence.

This verb means to encircle or surround something or someone. It describes movement or positioning around a person, place, or object, emphasizing that the surrounding boundary or group closes in on it. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 13 times across 13 verses, so its basic sense is consistent while the precise object being surrounded depends on the sentence. The word may describe people, structures, armies, or other things that form a circle around something. Its use stretches from Genesis through Jeremiah.

This Greek LXX word refers to a drink or to a drinking bout—a period or occasion centered on drinking. It functions as a noun, naming the drink or the drinking event rather than describing a person or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezra 3:7. The English rendering there is “drink,” consistent with its basic sense. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the way the sentence uses the noun.

This word means “problem”—a question, difficulty, or matter that calls for an answer or solution. It is a noun, so it names the problem itself rather than the act of questioning or solving it. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 10 times across 10 verses, especially in Judges 14, where it is used repeatedly in connection with Samson’s challenging question. Its broader use also appears in Psalms and Habakkuk, while the surrounding verse determines the particular problem being discussed.

“Nail to” is a verb describing the act of fastening one thing to another with a nail. It presents attachment as something done to an object, rather than merely being near it or touching it. This Greek LXX word occurs once in the available corpus, in 3 Maccabees 4:9. The reference identifies its sole recorded occurrence, while the basic meaning remains the action of nailing something to another surface or object.

This word means “soot,” the dark, powdery material produced by smoke or burning. It is a noun naming that substance rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Joel and Nahum, so its meaning is consistent but its precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage. The word therefore gives readers a concrete picture of blackened residue associated with fire or smoke, while the context determines how that picture functions in the passage.

This noun refers to a “deposit made by water”—material that water has built up or left in place. It describes a physical formation rather than an action, feeling, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in 2 Samuel 20:15 and 2 Kings 19:32. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic sense remains a water-formed deposit or accumulation.

Rabamag, also rendered Rhavamag, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named person or place in the Greek Old Testament tradition, but the available lexical information does not specify which. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Jeremiah 46:3. Its precise referent must therefore be understood from the surrounding verse and passage rather than from the name itself.

Salman is a proper name—the personal name of a man in the Greek Old Testament text. It is not a common word describing an action, quality, or object, so its meaning is primarily identifying rather than conceptual. In this LXX corpus, Salman appears twice, both times in Ruth 4:20–21. Scripture here supports recognizing Salman as a personal name rather than assigning it an added symbolic meaning.

Sebekatha, also rendered Sevekatha, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a person or name-bearing figure in the genealogy recorded at 1 Chronicles 1:9. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus. The available information establishes its name-form and location, but does not provide a separate lexical definition or enough surrounding verse text to explain more about the individual.

Sepphōra is a proper name, referring to a woman named Sepphōra in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general word describing an object, action, or quality, but a personal designation. This name occurs four times in the Greek translation of Exodus, appearing in four separate verses. Because the word itself is a name, its meaning is primarily identification: it points to the person called Sepphōra rather than expressing an additional concept. The surrounding verse is needed to explain what is happening whenever her name appears.

This word means “hardness”: the quality or condition of being hard. It is a noun, so it names that quality rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament (the LXX), it occurs four times across four verses, making it an occasional term rather than a common one. Its basic sense is compact and direct; the surrounding verse determines how that hardness is being applied. Without the verse wording, the clearest meaning is simply “hardness.”

This word means “carnelian,” a precious stone used to describe a material or object. It is an adjective, so it identifies something as having the character or appearance of carnelian rather than naming a person or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 29:2. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain exactly what it describes there.

This adjective describes someone or something that is mourned or that gives cause for grief. It points to a sorrowful condition, marking the person or thing as an object of mourning or as a source of deep sadness. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 5:15. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning is connected with mourning and grief.

This Greek Old Testament noun describes “taking together,” especially the act of seizing or arresting someone. It names a gathering or capture in which people are taken into custody or otherwise forcibly seized. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament, in Job, Jeremiah, and Hosea. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains an act of taking hold of someone or something.

This noun refers to something happening with or accompanying something else. It expresses association or concurrence rather than an independent action or object. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in the deuterocanonical book of 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning points to what accompanies or occurs together with another thing.

This Greek LXX noun means “sound of a pipe,” referring to the musical tone or noise produced by a pipe-like instrument. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Jeremiah 18:16. The word itself identifies a sound rather than a person, action, or abstract quality. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains the sound made by a pipe.

This Greek word means “cut.” It is a verb describing the act of cutting or dividing something with a physical action. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, it occurs ten times, including passages from Exodus, Leviticus, 2 Kings, Isaiah, Daniel, and 4 Maccabees. Its basic sense remains direct and practical: something is cut, rather than merely moved, changed, or removed. The precise force in any particular verse depends on what object is being cut and the surrounding sentence.

This word means “fourteenth.” It is an adjective that identifies something as occupying position fourteen in an ordered sequence, such as a numbered day, date, or other counted occasion. The word appears 27 times in the Greek LXX corpus, with occurrences from Genesis through 3 Maccabees. Its basic meaning remains an ordinal designation: it tells the reader that something comes after the thirteenth and before the fifteenth.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “shoot with the bow.” It describes the action of sending an arrow from a bow, whether as a command or as something someone did. The word appears eight times in the Greek Old Testament, in passages involving archery and the use of arrows. Its basic meaning remains focused and concrete: to shoot by means of a bow, rather than simply to strike or attack. The surrounding verse determines who performs the action and why.

This word means “this.” It is a pronoun used to point to a particular person, thing, or situation, usually one identified by the surrounding words. Its role is referential: it directs the reader’s attention to something specific rather than naming that thing by itself. The precise person or matter it identifies depends on the sentence and passage where it appears. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 872 times, showing that this is a common way to point out or identify something in the text.

e.t: “Fall brought by tripping up” or “stumble” is the meaning of this noun. It refers to a downfall understood as the result of being tripped or caused to stumble, rather than simply describing any fall. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Proverbs 24:17. The reference identifies its only occurrence, but the word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage.

This is a proper name referring to Phinees, also rendered Finees. It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, the name occurs 29 times, beginning in Exodus and continuing through 4 Maccabees. The name appears especially in passages connected with Israel’s priestly and historical records, but its basic meaning here is simply the personal name Phinees or Finees.

This Greek LXX verb means “knead”: to work a mixture by pressing and combining it, especially in preparing bread or a similar offering. It describes an action rather than an object or quality. The word occurs 13 times in the Greek Old Testament, with much of its use appearing in passages about preparing bread, cakes, or grain offerings. Its central sense remains the hands-on preparation of a mixture by kneading it.

This word means “potsherd,” a broken fragment of pottery or earthenware. It is a noun naming a physical object rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at Jeremiah 19:2. The word’s basic sense identifies a piece separated from a larger clay vessel; the surrounding passage is needed to understand why that object is mentioned there. Its recorded LXX use therefore points to a concrete pottery fragment, with no broader lexical sense established here.

Chorchor is a proper name, referring to a named place or people rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name is also rendered Khorkhor. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 27:16. Because the available wording does not include the surrounding verse, the name’s precise geographic or historical identification cannot be stated here. Its ordinary function is simply to identify the particular named entity mentioned in that passage.

This verb means “touch,” describing the act of making contact with someone or something. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 17:1. Its basic meaning is therefore straightforward: to touch or come into contact with something. The particular force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Onam is a personal name, identifying an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in 1 Chronicles 1:40. The name is given as “Ōnam; Onam.” The lexical information identifies its naming function but does not provide a separate descriptive meaning. Its particular significance in the genealogy depends on the surrounding passage and the person being named there.
